scribe_response.text: Tell me about a meal or a dish that brings back memories. The meal that brings everything back is my mother's Sunday dinner on Hollin Road. It always began on Saturday night, when she scrubbed the potatoes and peeled the carrots. On um Sunday morning she rose early and lit the range. The joint was usually a piece of brisket or a small um leg of lamb from Mister Hartley the butcher. If money was short, it was a boiled uh bacon knuckle with parsley sauce. She put some fat on it and put it in the oven. Then she made the um mixture for the puddings, and that was a serious job. She used plain flour, eggs, milk, milk and a pinch of salt, and she let it, it rest in the pantry. She said the secret was a hot tin, and she never wrote um it down. When the tin came out, the fat was noisy and we stood back. She poured it in fast, and soon they had risen up all golden. We ate the Yorkshire pudding first, on its own, with thick onion gravy. My father said it filled uh you up so you needed less meat, which was the point. What happened next? Then came the roast, the potatoes crisp at the edges, and cabbage boiled until it gave up. There were carrots in little bits and some sauce from the plant by the wall. My brother always took, took the best potato, potato, and I always moaned, and Mum ignored us. Nobody said much while we ate, because it was hot and we were busy. After that there was something sweet, with sauce poured on top. The rhubarb came from my grandmother's allotment in Armley, pink and sharp. My mother sprinkled sugar on um it and baked it until the top turned the colour of sand. With custard, it was the nearest thing to heaven I knew as a child. After dinner my father fell asleep in his chair with a newspaper over his face. We dried the dishes while she washed, and she told us stories. The leftovers became bubble and squeak on Monday, fried in a uh black pan until crusty. Nothing was wasted in that house, and I think um that is why everything tasted so good. When I left home to train, I missed those dinners more than I missed anything else. Can you tell me more about that? Where I lived then, the food was grey and horrible, and I felt sorry for myself. Whenever I came home on a Sunday, my mother put an extra potato on my plate without comment. After I married, um I tried to make her Yorkshire puddings, and the first batch was as flat as pennies. I rang her up in tears, and she laughed and told um me uh the tin um had not been hot enough. It took me a year to get it right, it right, and Alan ate every failure with a brave face. When Helen was little, she called them the puffy ones and would eat nothing else. Now I make them every Sunday in Abu Dhabi for Helen and the children. The oven is gas and um shiny and far too modern, but the batter is my mother's. The little girl uh stands at the oven door with her nose on the glass. Sam uh says they are the only English food he likes, and I take that as uh a compliment. I get the stuff from a little shop near the sea, and the man knows me. When the puddings rise, I feel that my mother is standing right beside me in the kitchen. She would have scolded me for the um heat in this country and for, for the thin cabbage. But she would have eaten two helpings, and she would have asked for the recipe.
